query: Explain increase prices impact on food security

sub_questions.question: Using the UN FAO SOFI 2023 and 2024 reports, explain how increases in food prices affect food security, including impacts on hunger, food insecurity, malnutrition, and the main transmission channels and drivers.

route.reason: The request is about the impact of rising prices on food security, which is directly covered by the FAO SOFI reports on hunger, food insecurity, malnutrition, and food prices.

csr.question: Using the UN FAO SOFI 2023 and 2024 reports, explain how increases in food prices affect food security, including impacts on hunger, food insecurity, malnutrition, and the main transmission channels and drivers.

answer.summary: SOFI 2023 and 2024 describe food-price increases as a core channel through which shocks reduce access to food: higher food, energy and input prices raise the cost of a healthy diet, squeeze real incomes, disrupt supply chains, and make nutritious foods less affordable. The effects show up in hunger remaining above pre-pandemic levels, elevated moderate/severe food insecurity, reduced diet quality, and risks of multiple forms of malnutrition. The reports emphasize that price shocks rarely act alone: conflict, climate extremes, economic slowdowns/downturns, inequality, unhealthy food environments and weak affordability of nutritious foods interact and compound impacts.

findings.claim: Food prices affect food security mainly through an affordability channel: when food prices rise faster than incomes, households’ economic access to food declines. SOFI 2023 defines affordability as the ability to buy foods locally, with diet cost assessed relative to income after other required expenses.

SOFI 2024 reports that food prices rose throughout 2022, increasing the global average cost of a healthy diet from 3.56 PPP dollars per person per day in 2021 to 3.96 PPP dollars in 2022; COVID-19 disruptions and the war in Ukraine contributed to higher international food and energy prices and inflationary pressure.

SOFI 2023 reports that the cost of a healthy diet rose globally by 4.3 percent, and that from 2020 to 2021 increases were larger in low- and middle-income countries: 6.2 percent in LMICs, 5.1 percent in UMICs, 4.7 percent in LICs, versus 2.1 percent in HICs.

Higher food prices contributed to unaffordability of healthy diets: SOFI 2023 estimates about 3.14 billion people, or 42 percent of the world population, could not afford a healthy diet in 2021, down from 3.19 billion, or 43 percent, in 2020.

The effect on hunger depends on the balance between income recovery and price inflation. SOFI 2023 explains that 2022 hunger trends reflected both an income effect from economic recovery and a price effect from high inflation; nevertheless hunger remained far above pre-pandemic levels globally and in all regions.

Regional impacts differed. In Southern Africa, increased hunger in 2022 stemmed from inflation after international commodity-price increases, plus unemployment and shock vulnerability; in Western Asia, conflict, political instability, disrupted supplies and high domestic inflation made access to food harder; in Southern Asia, sustained growth, especially in agriculture, likely outweighed inflation and improved food-security conditions.

Food-price increases can worsen malnutrition through diet-quality effects. SOFI 2024 states that food insecurity can be associated with lower consumption of all food types, a higher share of dietary energy from staples, lower consumption of nutritious foods, and/or higher consumption of energy-dense foods high in unhealthy fats, sugars and salt—pathways linked to undernutrition, micronutrient deficiencies, overweight and obesity.

SOFI 2024 frames price-related food insecurity as part of a broader driver system: conflict, climate variability and extremes, economic slowdowns/downturns, lack of access to and unaffordability of nutritious foods, unhealthy food environments, and high persistent inequality. These drivers are occurring more frequently, intensely and concurrently, especially in many low- and middle-income countries.

recommendations.action: Protect household purchasing power with targeted food or cash transfers indexed to local food-price inflation.
recommendations.why: This addresses the affordability channel: when prices rise relative to income, households lose access to healthy diets. Impact should be tracked through cost and affordability of a healthy diet and FIES moderate/severe food insecurity.

recommendations.action: Invest in resilient local and regional supply chains for nutritious foods, including storage, cold chains and logistics in climate- and conflict-exposed markets.
recommendations.why: SOFI links higher prices to supply disruptions from conflict, climate extremes, COVID-19 and the war in Ukraine; improving supply reliability can reduce price spikes and support access to diverse foods.

recommendations.action: Support smallholder productivity and market access for nutrient-dense foods, not only staple crops.
recommendations.why: Food insecurity affects diet quality, including reduced nutritious-food consumption and greater reliance on staples; production and market support for diverse foods can improve diet quality and affordability.

recommendations.action: Prioritize low- and middle-income countries and vulnerable regions where price increases and affordability pressures are highest.
recommendations.why: SOFI 2023 shows cost increases were much larger in LMICs, UMICs and LICs than in HICs, and regional examples show inflation interacting with unemployment, conflict and political instability.

recommendations.action: Use gender-, rural/urban- and income-disaggregated monitoring when designing programmes.
recommendations.why: SOFI 2024 notes higher food insecurity in rural areas than peri-urban and urban areas, and consistently higher food insecurity among women than men; price shocks can therefore have unequal effects.

next_steps: Map the company’s operating countries against SOFI risk drivers: conflict, climate extremes, economic slowdown, food inflation, inequality and unaffordability of healthy diets.
Identify workforce and community groups most exposed to food-price inflation, especially low-income households, women, rural communities and informal workers.
Select intervention geographies where food-price inflation and healthy-diet unaffordability are highest.
Define whether the CSR/ESG programme will focus on emergency purchasing power, resilient supply chains, nutritious-food production, or a combination.
Set a baseline for FIES food insecurity, cost/affordability of a healthy diet, dietary diversity and child nutrition indicators before programme launch.
Partner with local governments, food banks, producer groups and health/nutrition agencies to avoid duplicating existing social-protection or food-security programmes.

kpis.metric: Cost of a healthy diet and affordability of a healthy diet
kpis.how_to_measure: Track local cost of a least-cost healthy diet relative to household income; report change in the share of target households unable to afford it.

kpis.metric: Prevalence of moderate or severe food insecurity
kpis.how_to_measure: Use the Food Insecurity Experience Scale (FIES) in baseline and follow-up household surveys.
Measure household or individual dietary diversity and consumption frequency of nutritious foods versus staples and ultra-processed foods.
Track food consumption gaps, meal skipping, reduced portion sizes and, where available, prevalence of undernourishment at national or subnational level.
For relevant programmes, monitor child wasting, stunting, micronutrient deficiency proxies, and overweight/obesity risk indicators through health or nutrition partners.

Whether the focus is employees, supply-chain workers, smallholders, consumers or surrounding communities.

Existing partnerships with governments, NGOs, food retailers, farmers or health systems.

risks_assumptions: Confirmed SOFI findings describe global and regional patterns; local impacts may differ by market structure, policy response and household income sources.
Food-price increases can harm consumers but may benefit some net food-producing households if farmgate prices rise and input costs do not offset gains.
Cash or voucher support may be less effective where conflict, climate shocks or logistics constraints limit food availability.
Nutrition outcomes respond more slowly than food-price or food-security indicators and require health, sanitation and care-related interventions as well as food access.
Recommendations are programme hypotheses unless tailored with client-specific geography, population and budget data.

First, an income effect produced by the economic recovery in 2022 likely contributed to an increase in household disposable income and improved access to food, particularly for the poorest households that suffered heavy income losses during the pandemic. Globally, employment increased by 2.3 percent in 2022 from a meagre annual growth of 0.2 percent in the period from 2020 to 2021. 9 Employment growth was faster in low-income countries (LICs) and lower-middle-income countries (LMICs) than in upper-middle-income countries (UMICs) and high-income countries (HICs). Concomitantly, global unemployment declined significantly in 2022 to 205 million, down from 216 million in 2021 and 235 million in 2020, but still above its 2019 level. 9 The second factor affecting the trend in hunger is the price effect. Increases in food prices and general inflation can erode income gains and worsen access to food. In the short term, this is particularly true for the poorest segments of the population who spend a larger share of their income on food.

Assessing public domestic financing for food security and nutrition is problematic as there is no global financial database with sufficient data for the analysis. Public spending on agriculture is available globally, but this accounts for only a fraction, and sometimes a very small one, of all the public spending on food security and nutrition. There are not readily available data for all the countries in the world to estimate the public spending that is supporting food security and nutrition. An analysis of ten low- and middle-income countries shows that public spending on food security and nutrition was growing before the COVID-19 pandemic, with support to food consumption taking the greatest share, but this trend could not be sustained in some countries. Governments in some middle-income countries also seem to be spending relatively larger shares of their budget on addressing the major higher in poor countries affected by more than one major driver. Because agrifood systems in these countries are not resilient to these external forces, hunger, food insecurity and malnutrition are still on the rise and disproportionately affect children.

sources.text: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY The reverse in progress and the persistently high levels of hunger, food insecurity and malnutrition in recent years have put the world off track to meet Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) Targets 2.1 and 2.2 – to end hunger, food insecurity and all forms of malnutrition by 2030. Previous editions of this report have repeatedly highlighted the intensification of several major drivers of food insecurity and malnutrition, specifically conflict, climate variability and extremes, and economic slowdowns and downturns, combined with the well-established underlying factors that contribute to food insecurity and malnutrition, such as lack of access to and unaffordability of healthy diets, unhealthy food environments, and high and persistent inequality. Not only are these major drivers increasing in frequency and intensity, they are occurring concurrently more often, and in combination with the underlying factors, resulting in increasing numbers of hungry and food-insecure people. Depending on the major driver or combination of drivers affecting food security and nutrition in a country, addressing them will require a portfolio of policies across six transformative pathways, as outlined in detail in The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2021.
